Consider the following statements:
1. The matrix $\left(\begin{array}{ccc}1 & 2 & 1 \\ a & 2 a & 1 \\ b & 2 b & 1\end{array}\right)$ is singular.
2. The matrix $\left(\begin{array}{ccc}c & 2 c & 1 \\ a & 2 a & 1 \\ b & 2 b & 1\end{array}\right)$ is non-singular.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.solution:
A square matrix is said to be singular if its determinant is zero \& non-singular if its determinant is not equal to zero.
$\begin{aligned}
& \left|\begin{array}{ccc}
1 & 2 & 1 \\
a & 2 a & 1 \\
b & 2 b & 1
\end{array}\right|=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
1 & 2 & 1 \\
a-b & 2(a-b) & 0 \\
1-b & 2(1-b) & 0
\end{array}\right| \\
& \left\{\text { Applying } \mathrm{R}_2 \rightarrow \mathrm{R}_2-\mathrm{R}_3 ; \mathrm{R}_3 \rightarrow \mathrm{R}_1-\mathrm{R}_3\right\} \\
& =(a-b)(1-b)\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
1 & 2 & 1 \\
1 & 2 & 0 \\
1 & 2 & 0
\end{array}\right| \\
& =(a-b)(1-b)(2-2)=0 \text { It is singular. }
\end{aligned}\begin{aligned}
& \text { Again, }\left|\begin{array}{lll}
c & 2 c & 1 \\
a & 2 a & 1 \\
b & 2 b & 1
\end{array}\right|=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
c & 2 c & 1 \\
a-b & 2(a-b) & 0 \\
b-c & 2(b-c) & 0
\end{array}\right| \\
& \quad\left\{\text { Applying } \mathrm{R}_2 \rightarrow \mathrm{R}_2-\mathrm{R}_3 ; \mathrm{R}_3 \rightarrow \mathrm{R}_3-\mathrm{R}_2\right\} \\
& =(a-b)(b-c)\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
c & 2 c & 1 \\
1 & 2 & 0 \\
1 & 2 & 0
\end{array}\right| \\
& =(a-b)(b-c)(2-2)=0
\end{aligned}$
It is singular.

questions.q: What angle does the line segment joining $(5,2)$ and $(6,-15)$ subtend at $(0,0)$ ?
questions.solution:
Let point $\mathrm{A}=(5,2), \mathrm{B}=(6,-15)$ and $\mathrm{O}=(0,0)$.
Slope of line $\mathrm{OA}=m_1=\frac{2-0}{5-0}=\frac{2}{5}$
Slope of line $\mathrm{OB}=m_2=\frac{-15-0}{6-0}=\frac{-15}{6}$
Angle between two lines with slopes $m_1$ and $m_2$ is
$\begin{aligned}
\tan (\theta) & =\frac{m_1-m_2}{1+m_1 \cdot m_2} \\
& =\frac{\frac{2}{5}-\left(-\frac{15}{6}\right)}{1+\frac{2}{5} \cdot\left(-\frac{15}{6}\right)}=\frac{\frac{2}{5}+\frac{15}{6}}{1-1} \\
\tan (\theta) & =\infty \Rightarrow \theta=\frac{\pi}{2}
\end{aligned}$
